Chapter 3: State and Government

Government is formed to run the system of a state. This government works for the welfare of the state and citizens. Different government systems are established in the world, including monarchy, dictatorship, democracy etc. But democracy is the best government system among them all because it is the government of the people. Here people elect their representatives through vote.
Think and Answer!
What is the difference between monarchy and democracy? • Name any three advantages of democratic government.
Need of Federal Government

The Islamic Republic of Pakistan is a federation of four provinces (Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan), Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Gilgit Baltistan and the Capital Territory Islamabad. The federal government is a central government which runs the system of the entire country. This government controls the economy, defence, foreign affairs and other important national matters.
Need of Federal Government
The federal government formulates foreign policy, represents the country at the international level and develops friendly relations with other countries.
Formation of Government at Federal, Provincial and Local Level
A government has many levels, like federal, provincial and local. Let us learn about the formation of government at the federal, provincial and local levels.
Federal Government

Pakistan has the federal system of government. The people of Pakistan elect members of federal, provincial and local institutions. The members of the National Assembly elect the Prime Minister of Pakistan. The Prime Minister is the head of the federal government. The Prime Minister forms his cabinet to run the affairs of the federal government.
Federal Government

This cabinet consists of ministers, who are the heads of different ministries like finance, law, defence, interior and foreign affairs. The Prime Minister leads these ministries. The President is the head of state. The President is elected by the members of parliament and the provincial assemblies.
Federal Government

The federal government has three branches: the Legislature (Parliament — the President, the Senate and the National Assembly), the Executive (the Prime Minister, the Cabinet and administrative units) and the Judiciary (the Supreme Court and the Islamabad High Court).
Provincial Government

Every province has its own provincial government in Pakistan. The Chief Minister is the head of the provincial government. Provincial assemblies elect their Chief Ministers. The Chief Minister forms the provincial cabinet. The provincial government supervises provincial matters and ensures the basic rights of education, health, life and property of the citizens.
Provincial Government

Education, health, industry, agriculture, transport and many other departments come under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. In order to maintain law and order and facilitate people at grass-roots level, the provincial government forms local governments.
Provincial Government

The provincial government has three branches: the Legislature (the Provincial Assembly and the Governor), the Executive (the Chief Minister, the Cabinet and administrative units) and the Judiciary (the High Court).
Courts in Gilgit Baltistan and AJK
The Supreme Court is known as the "Supreme Appellate Court" whereas the High Court is known as the "Chief Court" in Gilgit Baltistan. Azad Jammu and Kashmir has a Supreme Court and a High Court.
Local Government

Local government is the third level of government after the central and provincial governments. A government that looks after a city, town or district and makes decisions in this regard is known as local government. It includes the Mayor, Chairman, Councillor etc. They work according to the rules and regulations of the provincial government.
Local Government

Local developmental works come under the jurisdiction of the provincial government, which provides powers, resources and funds to the local bodies for developmental works. Local government has a special structure in every province. Government is working to improve the system of local governments.
Interdependence of Federal, Provincial and Local Governments

Federal and provincial governments are formed after general elections, which are held every five years. According to the Constitution of Pakistan, federal and provincial governments have delegated powers. All federal developmental programmes are finalized according to the policies of parliament. Federal and provincial governments work together with coordination.
Interdependence of Federal, Provincial and Local Governments

The federal government plays the role of a bridge among provincial governments. It is responsible for national and international matters. Provincial governments work for the welfare of their respective provinces, whereas local government controls matters at district level.
Interdependence of Federal, Provincial and Local Governments

Provincial governments are autonomous in some matters, but some matters are settled by both governments; for example, the distribution of national resources for national and provincial developmental works is decided by both. Let us learn about the powers of local, provincial and federal governments with the help of a table.
Interdependence of Federal, Provincial and Local Governments

Federal Government | Provincial Government | Local Government; Controls national defence (matters of armed forces) | Controls law and order of the province (legislation regarding law and order) | Removes encroachments from roads and streets, arranges cattle markets and public fairs; Takes care of the economy of the country | Handles provincial taxes | Administers drinking water and sanitation; Supervises foreign policy (relations with other countries) | Controls provincial interior policy | Helps widows, orphans, the handicapped and affectees of natural disasters
Importance of Constitution

We live in a democratic and Islamic country. Its constitution has been formulated according to Islamic principles. Currently the 1973 Constitution is implemented in Pakistan. According to the constitution, the name of Pakistan is the "Islamic Republic of Pakistan", and Islam is the state religion, as Muslims are in the majority.
Importance of Constitution
The followers of other religions also live here, who have been given basic rights according to the constitution.
Constitution
A constitution is a combination of basic laws and principles according to which the system of government is run in a country or state.
For Teachers

Tell students about the need and importance of federal government, how federal and provincial governments work together to run the system of the country, the functions of the three pillars of government, and the structure of local, provincial and federal governments. Make students understand the concept of an "Islamic Republic State".
For Teachers
Tell them that government representatives are elected through elections in a democracy, and tell them about the functions of political parties and the names of a few current political parties.
Importance of Constitution

Urdu is the national language of Pakistan. The constitution provides guidance for running the affairs of a country or state. It provides laws for the government and government institutions (legislature, executive and judiciary) and determines the powers of these institutions. The constitution ensures the provision and protection of basic human rights. It also makes people aware of their responsibilities.
Do you want to know more?
Three different constitutions (1956, 1962 and 1973) have been implemented in Pakistan.
Rights and Duties of a Citizen According to the 1973 Constitution
According to the 1973 Constitution, the rights and responsibilities of Pakistani citizens are as below.
Rights of Citizens

Protection of life and property is the right of every citizen without any discrimination. • Every citizen has the right to live according to his beliefs. • Every citizen has the right to do business or trade, or adopt any other profession. • Freedom of expression and speech is the right of every citizen. • Every citizen has the right to buy, keep and sell property.
Rights of Citizens

• Every citizen has the right to travel, participate in gatherings and form a party in the country. • According to the constitution, child labour (of children under 14 years) is forbidden. • It is the responsibility of the government to impart free and compulsory education to children aged 5 to 16 years.
Stop and Tell
Which citizen's rights do you have?
Let's do something new!
Give suggestions to control child labour.
Responsibilities of Citizens
Citizens have some responsibilities as well as rights. For example:
Responsibilities of Citizens

They should be loyal to the country and in the time of need they should play their role in the defence of the country. • They should cast their vote correctly. • They should respect and obey national laws. • They should pay taxes on time. • They should respect the rights, beliefs and opinions of others. • They should protect public property.
Social Justice

Social justice means the provision of citizen and human rights to the people on the basis of equality. Social injustice is created due to the non-provision of such rights. Pakistan has many social injustices, like the lack of a uniform education system, unemployment and child labour etc. The current government is trying to tackle and put an end to these issues.
Importance of the Rule of Law

All the laws of the country are formulated according to the constitution. All citizens are equal in law; that is why the laws of the country are applied to all citizens in the same manner. People who break the law or indulge in any illegal activity are punished according to the law.
How courts work

The hearing of any trial is, first of all, conducted at a session or civil court. The judges of these courts are called session or district judges. If the two parties to a trial do not agree with the verdict of these courts, they can appeal to the High Court against the decision. The four provinces of the country have High Courts. The Chief Justice is the head of the High Court.
How courts work

The parties can appeal to the Supreme Court against the decision of the High Court if that decision is also not accepted. The Supreme Court is the apex court of the country. Its head is called the Chief Justice of Pakistan. The verdict of the Supreme Court is final.
Political Parties

A country has different political parties. Every political party has its own ideology and manifesto which make it popular among people. Every political party has a leader who makes it active and functional. After the election, the winning political party forms its government. Pakistan is a democratic country.
Political Parties

People elect their representatives through votes in a democratic system, and these representatives take control of government affairs after the election. These representatives belong to different political parties.
Functions of Political Parties
Let us learn about the functions of political parties.
Functions of Political Parties

Political parties work according to their manifestos. • They gather people on a platform and create political awareness among them. • They take part in elections and try to solve the problems of the people after being elected. • They work for the welfare of the country and nation after the formation of government. • They represent the country at the international level.
I have learnt!

Federal, provincial and local governments work together to run the system of a country. • The constitution is a combination of laws and basic principles according to which the affairs of a country are run. • Presently the Constitution of 1973 is implemented in Pakistan.

The Beginning of Civilizations

As human life passed through its developmental stages, it became more and more civilized. People adopted a better lifestyle, and thus human civilization began. Man passed through different phases of development and moved ahead. He adopted new ways of leading life. Social process came into existence. States and governments were formed and human civilization had a new beginning.

Common Era (CE)
The era after the birth of Hazrat Isa (AS) is called the Common Era.
Before the Common Era (BCE)
The period before the birth of Hazrat Isa (AS) is called Before the Common Era.
The Beginning of Civilizations
In this lesson, we will learn about the following three civilizations, of which the Greek civilization is the oldest: the Greek civilization, the Roman civilization and the Gandhara civilization.
Greek Civilization (1200 BC–146 BC)

The Greek civilization evolved about four thousand years ago along the banks of the Mediterranean Sea. Ancient Greece consisted of parts of Europe and most of the regions of western Asia. This region was famous throughout the world for its high mountains, large seas and beautiful islands.
Greek Civilization (1200 BC–146 BC)
Ancient Greece was divided into city-states. These included Athens, Sparta, Thebes and Olympia. These city-states had their own governments, laws and armies.
Greek Civilization (1200 BC–146 BC)

Athens and Sparta were the two important cities of ancient Greece. They were often at war against each other, but sometimes they would unite to defend Greece against foreign attacks. The cultures of these two states were completely different from each other: the Spartans loved wars and fighting, while the Athenians were interested in arts and education.
Greek Civilization (1200 BC–146 BC)

Ancient Greeks worshipped many gods and goddesses. They considered Zeus the supreme god and the ruler of all gods and goddesses. They had built temples in every city for worship, which were looked after by special people. The Greeks built their public buildings and temples on pillars. They had built large theatres for dramatic performances.
Greek Civilization (1200 BC–146 BC)
Greek houses consisted of a lawn and some rooms around it; each room had ventilators.
Greek Civilization (1200 BC–146 BC)
Most of the Greeks at that time did farming, fishing and trading. Moreover, many were soldiers, scholars, scientists and artists as well.
Chiton
The chiton was the dress of the ancient Greeks. It was a rectangular piece of cloth which the Greeks would tie with brooches on their shoulders and with belts around their waists.
Do you want to know more?
Famous philosophers such as Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, and the warrior Alexander the Great, belonged to the Greek civilization.
For Teachers
Students should be taught about the ancient civilizations of Greece, Rome and Gandhara with the help of documentaries. They should be informed about their salient features.
Parthenon Temple
The Parthenon temple, in the city of Athens in Greece, is a cultural symbol of old Greek culture on the Acropolis.
Marathon

The marathon originated in Greece and was started by a man called Pheidippides. He ran from Marathon to Sparta, covering a 150-mile distance, to inform his army about the Persian attack and ask for their help. The Greeks won that war because of him. To declare the victory, he ran from Marathon to Athens for 25 miles. The Greeks considered him their hero.
Olympic Games

Olympic games were introduced to the world by the ancient Greeks. These games started in the Greek city of Olympia in 776 BC. They were called the Olympics because of the city of Olympia. They included the marathon, wrestling and boxing. Modern Olympic games started in Greece in 1896 AD.
Olympic Games

Timeline of ancient Greeks: 776 BC — origin of the first Olympic games; 490 BC — Greeks defeated the Persians in the Marathon wars; 431–404 BC — wars between Athens and Sparta; 335 BC — Alexander the Great started his conquests; 323 BC — death of Alexander the Great; 146 BC — the Romans conquered Greece.
Roman Civilization (753 BC–476 AD)

The Roman civilization was one of the largest and most powerful civilizations of the world. It originated in 753 BC in Rome, which was a small town; now it is a large city in Italy near Greece. Rome was founded by its first king, Romulus. The Romans started expanding their empire through the use of force. They conquered Greece in 146 BC.
Roman Civilization (753 BC–476 AD)
They conquered all regions around the Mediterranean Sea and European regions, including England, Wales and Scotland, till 117 AD, and established their government in these regions.
Colosseum
The Colosseum was a great theatre in Rome built for holding different contests. It could accommodate about 50,000 people. It is still visited by people from all over the world.
Roman Civilization (753 BC–476 AD)

Ancient Rome had a diverse society. Different people worshipped their own gods and goddesses, and also worshipped spirits. They spoke Latin. They introduced the system of Roman numerals, which is still in use, and English letters are greatly influenced by the Roman alphabet. The Romans were hard-working and intelligent.
Roman Civilization (753 BC–476 AD)

They were attached to different professions such as farming, masonry, defence, trade, workmanship, law, teaching and artistry. There was an established government system which offered regular jobs to people.
Tunic and Toga
The tunic was a special dress of ancient Rome. It consisted of two woollen sewn shawls. The toga was a long shawl which they wrapped around the body.
Roman Civilization (753 BC–476 AD)

The Romans were great engineers and builders. They made arches and domes in their buildings. They built channels to bring water to their houses. They constructed very large buildings, which included amphitheatres, bath houses and multi-storey apartments. The head of the family in the Roman civilization was the most aged person, who had the power of decision about each member of his family.
Roman Civilization (753 BC–476 AD)

Timeline of ancient Rome: 753 BC — the first Roman king Romulus founded the city of Rome; 509 BC — democracy (the republic) started in Rome; 27 BC — the Roman Empire was established; 64 — most of the Roman region burnt in a fire; 80 AD — the Colosseum was constructed; 395 AD — Rome was divided into two empires; 476 AD — the end of the Roman Empire.
Gandhara Civilization (600 BC–500 AD)

Gandhara is the name of an ancient state. This region included Peshawar and the valleys of the River Swat and the River Kabul. Gandhara was a trade route between India, Central Asia and the Middle East in ancient times. It remained under Persian influence from 522 BC to 486 BC. A Greek warrior, Alexander the Great, conquered it in 327–326 BC. After Alexander, it came under the control of the Mauryan dynasty of India.
Gandhara Civilization (600 BC–500 AD)

Chandragupta Maurya was the famous king of this period. He established the first central government over most of the regions of the subcontinent. Handicrafts and other arts were greatly developed during his period. Different professions, including mining, trade, farming, sailing, transportation and revenue, were established. A canal system was also established in this period.
Gandhara Civilization (600 BC–500 AD)
Bactrian Greeks ruled this region in 185 BC after the Mauryan dynasty. The important cities of the Gandhara civilization were Purushapura (current Peshawar) and Takshashila (current Taxila).
Gandhara Civilization (600 BC–500 AD)

Hinduism was the most prominent religion of this region before the Persian occupation. Later on, Buddhism was made the state religion, and it remained here for about one thousand years. The most active role in its propagation was played by Ashoka, the grandson of Chandragupta Maurya. He built Buddhist stupas and sent Buddhist missionaries to preach in different regions of Asia.
Gandhara Civilization (600 BC–500 AD)

He inscribed the messages of Buddhism on routes, minarets and mountains. Buddhism spread to Tibet, China, Mongolia and Japan in his period. Gandhara was destroyed by Central Asian nomads in the fifth century AD. These nomads were called the "White Huns".

Buddhism began in the Indian city of Banaras. Gandhara was an important centre of art and education.
Gautama Buddha

Gautama Buddha was the founder of Buddhism. He was born in Nepal. He preached Buddhism for about forty-five years. He was a philosopher, a teacher and a religious leader. According to his philosophy, the only way to attain peace in this life and the life after death is to live a pious life, to take pity on all living things and not be cruel to others.
Gandhara Art

Gandhara art is famous all over the world. Different nations had ruled over the Gandhara civilization; therefore the influences of the Greek, Syrian, Persian and Indian civilizations are found in Gandhara art. The people of Gandhara made statues of Siddhartha Gautama Buddha, the founder of Buddhism, from stone and sand. They inscribed his pictures on rocks, buildings and monasteries.
Gandhara Art
The ruins of a Buddhist monastery are present in Takht-i-Bahi, Mardan (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) even now.
Gandhara Art

Timeline of Gandhara: 522–486 BC Persian rule; 500 BC Gautama Buddha's life; 327–326 BC rule of Alexander the Great; 321–297 BC Chandragupta Maurya's rule; 268–240 BC rule of Ashoka; 185 BC rule of the Bactrian Greeks; 1st century AD Kushan Empire; 5th century AD attack of the White Huns.

The Particular Individual Affecting History

The Holy Nabi Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ came at a time when all humanity was in darkness. Idol worship was at its peak. The Egyptian, Indian, Babylonian, Nineveh, Greek and Chinese civilizations were almost dead. The Arabs were divided into tribes, and there was no central government. Only the Roman and Persian kingdoms were alive, but people were living a life worse than animals in these kingdoms.
The Particular Individual Affecting History
The collective life of the people changed due to the teachings of the Holy Nabi ﷺ — from the masjid to the bazaar, from the madrassa to the court and from the house to the battlefield.
The Particular Individual Affecting History

Every aspect of mind, thinking, habits and manners, customs and usages, rights and duties, bad and good, permitted and forbidden (halal and haram), ethical values, laws and constitution, war and peace, economy, and marital manners and traditions was completely changed. The teachings of the Holy Nabi ﷺ are constructive rather than destructive. In short, he ﷺ turned the streams of civilization, history and culture.
The Particular Individual Affecting History
It is evident from history that the struggle for the creation of an independent state for the Muslims of the subcontinent was the result of this ideological and practical revolution.
Historical Personalities of Pakistan

There are a number of people in the world who are distinguished from others because of their courage, determination and boldness. When they determine to do something, they achieve it. Their achievements affect others, and they become famous throughout the world due to these qualities. They are called historical personalities. One such historical personality is Quaid-e-Azam. He was determined to achieve Pakistan.
Historical Personalities of Pakistan
He carried out his determination with the help of the other Muslims of the subcontinent. It is due to his struggle that today we live in a free Muslim state of our own.

Role of Provinces in the Creation of Pakistan
Each region of Pakistan played a vital role in the movement for independence. Let us study the role of these regions.
Sindh

The Muslims ruled over the subcontinent for about nine hundred years. Their rule continued until the dominance of the British, who occupied most of the regions of the subcontinent slowly and gradually. The British occupied Sindh in 1843. They annexed it to Bombay and started using it for their administrative affairs.
Sindh
Quaid-e-Azam struggled very hard for separating Sindh from Bombay because he knew it was necessary for protecting the rights of Muslims. Sindh was made a separate province in 1936.
Sindh

A meeting of the provincial Muslim League of Sindh was held in Karachi in 1938, presided over by Quaid-e-Azam. A resolution was passed in this meeting for the establishment of an independent state for Muslims; Sindh was the first province which passed such a resolution. This resolution was presented by Sheikh Abdul Majeed Sindhi.
Sindh

Prominent leaders of Sindh were Quaid-e-Azam, Fatima Jinnah, Begum Abdullah Haroon, Sir Abdullah Haroon, Begum Rana Liaquat Ali Khan, G. Allana and Muhammad Ayub Khoro. Students, religious leaders and traders also played an important role, along with political leaders, in creating awareness among the people of Sindh for the creation of an independent Muslim state.
Sindh

Students of the Sindh Muslim Student Federation and Sindh Madrassatul Islam actively participated in the Pakistan Movement. The people of Sindh supported the Pakistan Resolution. The provincial assembly of Sindh formally declared Sindh a part of Pakistan on June 26, 1947; Sindh became the first province to be included in Pakistan because of this decision.
Punjab

The province of Punjab has remained a centre of political activities. Sir Mian Muhammad Shafi established the Punjab Muslim League in 1906 to unite the Muslims of Punjab. In the politics of Punjab, Dr. Allama Muhammad Iqbal, Sir Mian Muhammad Shafi and Malik Barkat Ali played an important role.
Punjab
They favoured separate elections for the Muslims of the subcontinent so that the separate identity of the Muslims could be established.
Punjab

In 1930, Allama Iqbal proposed the division of the subcontinent on the basis of the Two Nation Theory in his address at Allahabad. Quaid-e-Azam came back from England at the request of Muslim leaders and took the responsibility of leading them. The annual session of the All India Muslim League was held at Minto Park, Lahore, on 23rd March 1940.
Punjab

A resolution was presented in this meeting for the establishment of a separate state for the Muslims; it was titled the "Pakistan Resolution". The students of Punjab did exemplary work for the creation of Pakistan; the Punjab Muslim Students Federation spread the message of Quaid-e-Azam to the cities and towns of Punjab. Due to the struggle of Quaid-e-Azam,
Punjab
Muslim-majority areas of Punjab were declared part of Pakistan on June 3, 1947.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was the last region that the British brought under their control. The people of this region were against British rule and never surrendered to the British. As a result, the British rulers never gave any importance to the development of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and tried their best to keep the people away from politics.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

The people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa started raising their voice for their rights with the beginning of the movement for independence in the subcontinent. Sir Sahibzada Abdul Qayyum Khan founded Islamia College Peshawar and the Collegiate School in 1913. These institutions created political awareness among the Pashtoons.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

The students of Islamia College Peshawar actively participated in the Pakistan Movement and supported the "Pakistan Resolution". Sardar Aurangzeb Khan, Begum Zari Sarfaraz, Mian Zia-ud-Din, Bahadar Saadullah Khan and others represented the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in passing the "Pakistan Resolution".
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Sardar Abdur Rab Nishtar was one of the prominent leaders of the Pakistan Movement. He served as a member of the Legislative Assembly of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and also as the finance minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. After the announcement of the partition of the subcontinent, a referendum was held in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in July 1947 to know the will of the people about joining Pakistan or India.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
The majority of the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa voted in favour of Pakistan in this referendum, and thus it became a province of Pakistan.

A squad of volunteers from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa served on the security of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah in the meeting of March 1940.

Quaid-e-Azam and Islamia College

Quaid-e-Azam visited Islamia College Peshawar in 1936. He was given life honorary membership of the Khyber Union of Islamia College. On this occasion, Quaid-e-Azam donated one-third of his property to Islamia College Peshawar.
Balochistan

Balochistan is home to the ancient civilization of Mehrgarh. The remains of this civilization have been discovered in the Bolan Pass, Quetta and Sibi. The people of this region are naturally freedom lovers and never accepted slavery. This region was more backward compared with other regions of the subcontinent, and the Pakistan Movement started here very late.
Balochistan

On the directives of Quaid-e-Azam in 1939, Qazi Muhammad Isa strengthened the Balochistan Muslim League. Begum Saeeda Qazi, wife of Qazi Muhammad Isa, actively participated in the Pakistan Movement; she was very active in arranging a meeting on the arrival of Quaid-e-Azam in Quetta. Personalities like Fazal Ahmad Ghazi, Malik Abdullah Jan Kasi and Fateh Muhammad guided the people of Balochistan.
Balochistan

The people of Balochistan supported the Pakistan Resolution of 1940. The Shahi Jirga of Balochistan decided to join Pakistan; Nawab Muhammad Khan Jogezai and Mir Jafar Khan Jamali showed great enthusiasm in taking this decision.
Gilgit Baltistan

When the Pakistan Movement was at its peak, Gilgit Baltistan was under the control of the Maharaja. According to the 3rd June Plan, all independent states of the subcontinent were given the option to decide whether to join Pakistan or India. Maharaja Hari Singh decided to join India against the will of the people.
Gilgit Baltistan

In reaction to this decision, the soldiers of the Gilgit Scouts and the Kashmir 6th Infantry started a rebellion against the Maharaja, led by Mirza Hasan Khan, Babar Khan, Shah Khan and others. They dismissed the government of Governor Ghansara Singh on November 1, 1947 and declared the independence of Gilgit Baltistan.
Gilgit Baltistan

They hoisted Pakistan's flag at Scout Line on November 2, 1947 and established a provincial government there; Shah Raees Khan was appointed president and Mirza Hasan Khan commander-in-chief. Sardar Muhammad Alam Khan arrived in Gilgit on November 16, 1947 and took control of the administration, and Gilgit Baltistan came under the control of the Government of Pakistan.
Azad Jammu and Kashmir

Jammu and Kashmir was an independent state at the time of the partition of the subcontinent. It was a Muslim-majority state. The wave of independence in the subcontinent also influenced the people of Jammu and Kashmir. Syed Zia-ud-Din Indrabi was a famous leader of the Pakistan Movement; he represented the delegation of Kashmiris in the meeting of March 23, 1940 and supported the Pakistan Resolution.
Azad Jammu and Kashmir

Chaudhry Ghulam Abbas was also a prominent leader of Kashmir. At the time of partition, independent states were given the option to decide whether to join India or Pakistan or retain their independent status. Kashmiris wanted to join Pakistan, but Maharaja Hari Singh, the ruler of Jammu and Kashmir, decided to annex the state to India on October 26, 1947.
Azad Jammu and Kashmir
Due to this, some Kashmiris started jihad against the Maharaja. They freed a part of Kashmir and annexed it to Pakistan.

Globe and Map Skills

Maps are used to find places. A map is the pictorial sketch of the Earth or any part of the Earth. A map can be of a school, a house, a city, a town or a country. Using maps, we can find water resources such as rivers and oceans.
Map

The representation of the Earth or any part of it on plain paper is called a map. Maps are made for different purposes with different scales. Maps can be taken easily from one place to another. The elements of a map are called "BOLTS". You studied the elements of a map in class 4.
BOLTS
B = Border, O = Orientation, L = Legend, T = Title, S = Scale
Map

The distribution map above shows all five elements: its title ("Distribution Map — Important Industries of Pakistan"), the scale bar (0–200–400 km), the orientation (compass rose), the border round the map, and the legend (textile, sugar, cement, automobile and cottage industries).
Border
Map borders are the lines on all four sides of a map which enclose it like a picture frame. A border is also called a hem.
Orientation
Finding directions on a map is called orientation. North, East, West and South are the four cardinal directions.
Stop and Tell
Tell the names of the intermediate directions.
Legend
The features of the Earth, such as mountains, plains, deserts, trees, buildings and roads, are shown by special signs on maps. These signs are given in a list on the map, which is called the legend.
Do you want to know more?
Signs are also called conventional signs.
Title
A map is given a title, which is written on top of the map in bold and visible letters. It shows the area and purpose of the map.
For Teachers
Ask students about the term "BOLTS". Show them a map and ask them questions about its elements.
Scale
The distance on the ground and on the map is shown in a specific ratio; this is called the scale. With the help of the scale we can find the distance between two places on a map.
Types of Scale
There are three types of scale: (1) linear scale, (2) statement of scale, and (3) representative fraction (RF).
Types of Scale
(1) Linear scale: This scale is in the form of a horizontal line divided into equal parts. The line shows the ratio between ground distance and map distance.
Types of Scale
(2) Statement of scale: A statement of scale shows distances in words. For example, a distance of four miles is shown by one inch in the given scale (1 inch = 4 miles).
Types of Scale

(3) Representative Fraction (RF): A fraction is used to show distance on this scale. The numerator of the fraction is the unit (1), which shows the distance on the map; the denominator shows the distance on the ground. This scale is shown both as a fraction and as a ratio, for example 1/253,440 or 1 : 253,440.
Kinds of Map
A map has many kinds, such as: 1. political map, 2. tourist map, 3. weather map, 4. topographical map, and 5. road map. Let us read about these maps in detail.
1. Political Map
A map used for finding international borders, countries, capitals and important cities is called a political map.
2. Tourist Map
Tourist maps are made for tourists, who use them to get information about a place. These maps have detailed information about tourist spots, such as pictures of a place, important sites and roads.
For Teachers
Provide information about different types of maps to students with the help of pictures and maps. Tell them that each kind of map has a different purpose and use.
3. Weather Map
A weather map is used to show the weather conditions of an area at a particular time with the help of different signs.
4. Topographical Map

Topographical maps are used to show the features of the Earth such as mountains, valleys and plains. Physical features are shown with contour lines in these maps; these lines are used to show the altitude (height) of a place.
5. Road Map
A road map shows important places, highways, roads, railway lines etc.
Lines of Latitude and Longitude

The horizontal and vertical lines on a map are called a "grid". These are imaginary lines, which are called lines of latitude and longitude. These lines can be used to find the location of an area or place on a globe or map.
Lines of Latitude and Longitude

The world map shows the seven continents (North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia and Antarctica) and the oceans (Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Antarctic/Southern Ocean), with latitude lines marked 0° to 80° north and south and longitude lines marked 0° to 180° east and west.
Lines of Latitude

The imaginary horizontal lines on a map from east to west are called lines of latitude. The longest latitude line, situated at zero degrees, is called the Equator. It divides the Earth horizontally into two equal parts. Lines of latitude are parallel to the Equator. These lines are 180 in number: 90 lines of latitude are to the north and 90 to the south of the Equator.
Lines of Latitude
Lines of latitude can be used to find the distance between two places.
Lines of Longitude

The imaginary vertical lines on a globe or map from north to south are called lines of longitude. The line of 0° longitude is called the Prime Meridian, which passes through Greenwich in England. The Prime Meridian vertically divides the Earth into two equal parts. There are 360 lines of longitude: 180 are to the east and 180 to the west of the Prime Meridian.
Lines of Longitude

With the help of lines of longitude we can find the difference of time between two countries. The Equator is an important line of latitude; similarly, the Prime Meridian is an important line of longitude.
Do you want to know more?
1 line (degree) of latitude = about 111 kilometres. 1 line (degree) of longitude = 4 minutes (of time).
Important Lines of Latitude

The Arctic Circle is 66.5° north of the Equator. • The Tropic of Cancer is 23.5° north of the Equator. • The Equator is at 0° latitude, which divides the Earth into two equal parts. • The Tropic of Capricorn is 23.5° south of the Equator. • The Antarctic Circle is 66.5° south of the Equator.
Time Zones

The Prime Meridian passing through Greenwich was accepted as the line of 0° at an international conference in 1884. The time of this place, Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), was accepted as standard time. Twenty-four time zones were made, which show the twenty-four hours of the day: twelve time zones to the east and twelve to the west of Greenwich.
Time Zones

Going eastwards from this point, each time zone gains one hour; similarly, going westwards from Greenwich, each time zone loses one hour. Look at the given map: Pakistan is located in the +5 time zone, so the time here is 5 hours ahead of Greenwich. If the time at Greenwich is 07:00 AM, the time in Pakistan will be 12:00 PM.
Time Zones
The Earth has been divided according to time into strips having 15 lines of longitude each, which are called time zones.
Do you want to know more?

The Earth turns through 15° of longitude per hour facing the sun, and completes 360° of longitude in one complete rotation. Each time zone consists of 15° of longitude. As there are 360 lines of longitude, there are 24 time zones: 360° ÷ 15° = 24.
Time Zones

Map of time zones: the zones to the west of the Prime Meridian (−1 to −12) are behind Greenwich time, and those to the east (+1 to +12) are ahead of it; the International Date Line runs along 180°, where the day changes (for example Sunday on one side and Monday on the other).
Do you want to know more?

am = ante meridiem (before noon), pm = post meridiem (after noon). A day of 24 hours consists of two parts. AM means before 12 o'clock: the 12 hours between 12 o'clock midnight and 12 o'clock noon are shown with "am". PM means after 12 o'clock: the 12 hours between 12 o'clock noon and 12 o'clock midnight are shown with "pm".
Time Zones

Let us find out the time of Lahore from Greenwich. To know the time of a place, it is necessary to know the line of longitude of that place. The line of longitude of Lahore is 75° east. If the time in Greenwich is 12:00 PM, what would be the time in Lahore?
Time Zones
The difference between the time of Lahore and Greenwich = (line of longitude of Lahore) ÷ 15° = 75° ÷ 15° = 5 hours
Time Zones

Since Lahore is situated to the east of Greenwich, its time will be 5 hours ahead of Greenwich. If the time in Greenwich is 12:00 PM, the time in Lahore will be 05:00 PM (12:00 + 5 = 17:00, i.e. 05:00 PM).
Do you want to know more?
The standard time of Pakistan is taken from Lahore.

Physical Features of Pakistan

Allah Almighty has endowed Pakistan with every type of physical feature. There are high mountain ranges, beautiful valleys, fertile plains, vast deserts and plateaus full of minerals. Besides, there are springs of fresh sweet water, waterfalls, lakes and rivers which add to the beauty of Pakistan. Viewers are enchanted by the deep seas and golden coasts of Pakistan.
Region
The area where the features of land, climate, plants and ways of living of people are similar is geographically called a region.
Think and Answer!
Where is the mountainous area of Pakistan situated? • Write the names of important deserts of Pakistan.
Pakistan (Physical Map)

The physical map shows the northern mountains (Karakoram, Himalayas, Hindu Kush with Tirich Mir, Nanga Parbat and the Khunjerab Pass), the western mountains (Sulaiman, Kirthar, Chaghi, Toba Kakar, Ras Koh, Wazirstan hills, Koh-e-Sufaid) with the Khyber, Gomal and Bolan passes, the Potwar Plateau and Salt Range, the Balochistan Plateau, the Upper and Lower Indus Plains, the deserts (Thal, Cholistan, Thar, Nara, Kharan), Hamun-e-Mashkhel, and the coastal areas (Makran Coast, Karachi Port, Gwadar).
Pakistan (Physical Map)
Let us read about the different physical regions of Pakistan.
Mountain Ranges

Mountain ranges start in the farthest north of Pakistan. The mountain ranges of Pakistan are divided into three parts: 1. the Northern Mountain Range, 2. the North Western Mountain Range, and 3. the Western Mountain Range.
Do you want to know more?

Some mountaineers and adventurers from Italy climbed to the top of a mountain peak under the guidance of Ardito Desio in 1954. Climbing to the top of that peak was very difficult because of the harsh weather and the steep slope of the peak, but these mountaineers made it possible. It was the peak of K-2, situated in Pakistan, which is the second-highest peak in the world.
1. Northern Mountain Range
The Northern Mountain Range consists of the Karakoram and Himalaya mountain ranges. Most of these ranges are covered with snow.
Karakoram

The Karakoram mountain range stretches from Gilgit to Skardu in the north of Pakistan. K-2 is the highest peak of this range. K-2 is also called "Godwin Austen", because the name of its first surveyor was Godwin Austen. Its height is 8,611 metres. The Siachen, Baltoro and Biafo glaciers are in this range. The Silk Road, which connects Pakistan with China, passes through this range.
Karakoram
Hunza, Skardu and Gilgit are located in it.
For Teachers

Tell students that a physical region consists of mountains, plains, deserts and other land types. Places which are higher than the ground level and have steep slopes on all sides are called mountains. A plateau is levelled land, higher than the plain, with slopes on each side. Plains are levelled areas with gentle slopes. A desert consists of sand dunes and receives very little rain.
For Teachers
The area near the sea is called the coastal region.
Himalayas

The Himalayan mountain range is situated to the south of the Karakoram. The highest peak of this range is Nanga Parbat. The height of Nanga Parbat is 8,126 metres; it is situated in Diamir district (Gilgit). The Himalayan Mountain Range consists of the Greater Himalayas, the Lesser Himalayas and the Siwalik Hills. The valleys of Murree, Nathiagali, Ayubia and Kaghan are situated in this range.
Greater Himalayas
The Greater Himalayas consist of the high mountain ranges of Swat, Kohistan and Gilgit Baltistan. The average height of this range is about 6,000 metres.
Lesser Himalayas
The Lesser Himalayas consist of the mountain ranges of Azad Kashmir and Pir Panjal. The average height of this range is about 4,000 metres.
Siwalik Hills
The Siwalik Himalayas consist of the less high mountains of Islamabad, Abbottabad and a few hills of Hazara. The average height of these mountains is about 800 metres.
Do you want to know more?
The Northern, North Western and Western mountain ranges join one another on the Pamir plateau. This place is called the Pamir Knot.
2. North Western Mountain Range
This mountain range includes the Hindu Kush range.
Hindu Kush

The Hindu Kush range is situated in the north-western part of Pakistan along the border of Afghanistan. The highest peak of this range is Tirich Mir (Chitral); its height is 7,690 metres. The areas of Malakand, Swat and Chitral are situated in this range. It extends up to the Kabul River.
For Teachers

Show students the physical map of Pakistan and tell them about the locations of its physical regions. Also tell them that most of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa consists of mountain ranges, the provinces of Sindh and Punjab consist of plains, and the major part of Balochistan is plateau.
3. Western Mountain Range
The Western Mountain Range consists of the following mountain ranges:
Koh-e-Sufaid and Waziristan Hills

Koh-e-Sufaid is situated in the south of the Hindu Kush, between the Kabul River and the Kurram River. This mountain range is spread along the border of Afghanistan. The highest peak of this range is Sikaram. The Khyber Pass is an important pass of this mountain range, which connects Peshawar with Kabul. The narrow passage between two mountains is called a 'pass'.
Koh-e-Sufaid and Waziristan Hills

The Waziristan Hills are situated in the south of Koh-e-Sufaid. This mountain range is located between the Kurram River and the Gomal River. Kurram, Tochi and Gomal are some of the important passes of this mountain range.
Koh-e-Sulaiman and Kirthar Mountain

Koh-e-Sulaiman is located in the south of the Gomal River. This mountain range is situated between Balochistan and Punjab. The highest peak in this range is Takht-e-Sulaiman. Bolan is the name of an important pass in this mountain range. Kirthar Mountain is situated in the south of Koh-e-Sulaiman, between Balochistan and Sindh. The mountain ranges of Makran and Pab are situated to the west of Kirthar Mountain.
Ras Koh and Chaghi Hills
The Ras Koh and Chaghi Hills are situated in the west of Balochistan. The Chaghi Hills are situated on the Pak-Afghan border.
Plateaus
The land of Pakistan has two plateaus. These plateaus are full of coal, gas, sulphur and aluminium.
1. Potwar Plateau

The Potwar Plateau is situated between the River Indus and the River Jhelum. The plateau includes the districts of Jhelum, Chakwal, Attock and Rawalpindi. This plateau is eroded, sandy and barren due to rainfall and seasonal rills. It is not fit for cultivation; only those areas which are close to rivers are cultivated.
1. Potwar Plateau

But this area is full of different types of minerals such as limestone, coal, salt and mineral oil. The Salt Range is in the south of this plateau, where the Khewra mine is situated, which is the second largest salt mine in the world.
1. Potwar Plateau
The famous rivers of this area are the River Haro and the River Soan. Besides, there are many seasonal rills as well. The valleys of Soon, Sakesar and Kalar Kahar are also situated in this area.
2. Balochistan Plateau

The Balochistan Plateau is situated to the west of Koh-e-Kirthar and Koh-e-Sulaiman. This area has mostly barren and dry hills. The Central Makran Range, Siahan Range and Toba Kakar Range are the important mountain ranges of this plateau. This plateau is very important on account of minerals; its important minerals are natural gas, sulphur, copper and coal.
2. Balochistan Plateau

It has an extreme and dry climate, and it resembles a desert due to its dry climate and little rain. Those areas where water is available have orchards of apples, peaches, grapes and pomegranates. These orchards are irrigated with 'Karez' (underground water channels). The important rivers of this area are the River Zhob, River Porali, River Hingol, River Hub and River Dasht.
Plains
The plains of Pakistan are very fertile. The weather, water and soil of these plains are very suitable for farming. The plain region of Pakistan is divided into two parts:
1. Upper Indus Plain

The Upper Indus Plain consists mainly of the province of Punjab. It starts from the Potwar Plateau and stretches up to Kot Mithan. This region is also called the land of five rivers. This plain is made up of soft and fertile soil carried by rivers. These rivers include the River Indus, River Jhelum, River Chenab, River Ravi and River Sutlej.
1. Upper Indus Plain
Canals have been taken out from these rivers at certain places, which irrigate crops in this area.
2. Lower Indus Plain

Most of the area of Sindh and the southern part of the province of Punjab are called the Lower Indus Plain. It stretches from Kot Mithan to the Arabian Sea. The tributaries of the River Indus, which are the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi and Sutlej, meet the River Indus at Kot Mithan. The Indus flows alone from Kot Mithan to the Arabian Sea. This plain is very fertile and is irrigated by the River Indus and its canals.
2. Lower Indus Plain
The eastern part of this plain is desert.
Deserts
The deserts of Pakistan are extremely hot and sandy. The major deserts of Pakistan are the following.
Thal
The desert of Thal is situated between the River Indus and the River Jhelum. It consists of the districts of Khushab, Bhakkar, Jhang and Muzaffargarh.
Thar

The desert of Thar is situated in the eastern and south-eastern part of Sindh. It is the largest desert of Pakistan. The part of the desert which is in Sindh is called the 'Nara Desert'. It consists of the areas of Ghotki, Sanghar, Mirpur Khas and Tharparkar. The part of this desert in Punjab is called the 'Cholistan Desert', which includes the areas of Bahawalnagar, Bahawalpur and Rahim Yar Khan.
Kharan

Most of the Kharan Desert is situated in the district of Kharan in Balochistan. It consists of the western part of Balochistan. It is surrounded by small hills. Its weather is dry. It contains shrubs and thorny plants.
Do you want to know more?
A vast desert (Kharan) is situated between Chaghi and Siahan, where a lake of salt water is situated. This lake is called Hamun-e-Mashkhel.
Coastal Areas

The coastal area of Sindh and Balochistan stretches along the Arabian Sea. Its length is about 1,050 kilometres. This area has tourist places and ports. Karachi Port, Port Qasim and Keti Bandar are situated in the coastal area of Sindh. Karachi Port is the largest and busiest port of Pakistan. The coastal area of Balochistan has the ports of Gwadar, Pasni and Jiwani.
Coastal Areas

Gwadar port is expected to be the centre of the economic activities of Pakistan. It is an important part of the China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and an important port for the development of economic relations between Pakistan and China.
Lifestyle of the People in Different Regions
The lifestyle of the people of the different physical regions of Pakistan is different from each other. Let us read about the lifestyle of the people of Pakistan.
Let's do something new!

Draw a sketch of the map of Pakistan on a chart with your friends. Use different colours to show the different physical regions of Pakistan: brown for the mountain ranges, green for the plain regions, yellow for plateaus, orange for deserts and blue for coastal regions.
1. Mountainous Region

The mountainous regions of Pakistan are very cold in winter due to frequent snowfall. The people of these areas wear thick woollen clothes to protect themselves from the extreme cold. Summer is moderate. Raising sheep and goats is the main profession of the people of this area. Another major source of income is tourism. Farming is the profession of the people living in valleys.
2. Plateaus

People who live on the plateaus of Pakistan face intense heat in summer and cold in winter. But mineral resources are abundant in these regions; therefore, most of the people are miners. Farming is also carried out in some areas. People wear loose cotton clothes due to the hot weather.
2. Plateaus

At some places on the Balochistan Plateau, people bring drinking water from distant places, while at some places people use pond water for drinking because clean water is not available. The karez system is used for irrigation.
3. Plain Areas

The people of plain areas are mostly farmers. Some of the people are attached with industries as well. The plain areas of Pakistan are thickly populated. Some of the reasons for the thick population in these areas are fertile land, suitable weather and climate.
Stop and Tell
How is the lifestyle of the people of the plains of Pakistan similar to or different from the people of the plateaus?
4. Desert Areas

The desert areas of Pakistan are extremely hot. These areas are not suitable for farming due to sand and scarcity of water. The people of these areas live like nomads. They raise sheep and goats for earning their bread. Camels are also raised here.
5. Coastal Areas

The coastal area of Pakistan is the centre of economic activities due to its sea ports. Most of the people of these areas are attached with business and industries. Fishing is also an important profession. The climate of this area is moderate and the air is mostly moist.
5. Coastal Areas
Coastal areas are thickly populated, resulting in a scarcity of resources; for example, people face a shortage of drinking water, which creates many health problems for them.

When these average weather conditions remain constant in a particular region, it is called climate. The climate of many regions of the world is extremely cold, while the climate of some regions is extremely hot. The state of climate in these regions remains unchanged for many years.

Factors Affecting Climate

The weather of the different regions of the world is different. The climate of some regions is hot while it is extremely cold in other regions. There are many factors which affect the climate of different regions of the world. Let us study these factors.
Distance from the Equator

Temperature is high in those regions which are close to the Equator. The reason is that the sun's rays fall vertically over the Equator. For example, Ecuador, Brazil, Kenya and Indonesia are situated on the Equator. Those areas which are situated near the poles are very cold because the sun's rays fall slantingly over the poles. Canada, Denmark and Russia are situated near the North Pole.
Altitude

As we move to higher places, temperature decreases. Mountainous areas are higher than sea level; therefore, the climate of mountainous areas is cold. The climate of the plain areas is comparatively hot.
Altitude
Diagram: at 0 metres the temperature is 30°C, at 2,000 metres 17°C, and at 3,000 metres 10°C.

Why is there a significant difference between the climate of Murree and Karachi?
Ocean Currents

The continuous flow of water in the ocean is called a current. Generally, there are two types of ocean currents: warm water currents and cold water currents. The warm currents of the water increase or moderate the temperature of their coastal areas, while the cold water currents decrease the temperature of their coastal areas.
Direction of Winds

The winds blowing from the hot regions raise the temperature of the regions towards which they blow, whereas the winds blowing from the cold regions decrease the temperature. The winds from the oceans are generally moist and sometimes cause rainfall.
Effect of Human Activities on Climate
Besides these natural factors, some human activities also affect climate, which are given below:
Effect of Human Activities on Climate

Trees absorb carbon dioxide and emit oxygen. Cutting trees increases carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. • Factories use fuels such as petrol, coal and gas. Burning these fuels increases carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere. • The smoke emitted by vehicles and factories increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Effect of Human Activities on Climate
Scientists are of the view that carbon dioxide is the major cause of global warming. Let us study global warming.
Global Warming

The earth is enveloped in a cover of gases. This cover of gases is called the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide and other gases present in the atmosphere allow the sun's rays to reach the earth but prevent the heat of the earth from going out. These gases increase the temperature of the earth. This is called the Greenhouse Effect. The gases involved in the Greenhouse Effect are called Greenhouse Gases.
Global Warming
The increase in the temperature of the earth due to the Greenhouse Effect is called Global Warming.
Effects of Global Warming
Some of the effects of global warming are the following:
Effects of Global Warming
Melting of glaciers • Rise in the sea level • Extreme weather conditions • Increase in skin and breathing diseases
Do you want to know more?

The increase in temperature due to global warming also causes changes in weather. One example is the monsoon rain in Karachi in 2020, which caused floods in Karachi. These floods caused great human as well as financial loss. Karachi had never experienced such heavy rain in the past sixty to seventy years.
Effects of Global Warming

It is necessary to plant as many trees as possible to avoid these dangers. Besides, it is also necessary to reduce the poisonous gases emitted by industries and to use vehicles which emit less smoke. People must walk short distances on foot. Alternative resources of energy, such as solar and wind energy, must be used instead of coal and gas.

Natural Disasters

Those natural incidents and factors which cause damage to life and property on earth are called natural disasters. For example, cyclones, droughts, earthquakes, landslides and floods are some of the natural disasters. Let us study the causes and damages of natural disasters.
Cyclones
Sometimes the air pressure of a place decreases because of an increase in temperature, while the air pressure in the surrounding area is high.
Cyclones

As a result, the wind blows towards the low air pressure area from the high pressure areas and causes cyclones. These cyclones cause violent storms, rainfall and snowfall. They cause great human and financial losses. Trees are uprooted, which block roads, and crops are destroyed. Besides land, cyclones are also formed over oceans.
Landsliding

When rocks and mud of mountains move downwards due to the gravity of the earth, strong winds or heavy rain, it is called landsliding. Landsliding destroys everything in its way. Routes, roads and highways are blocked due to landsliding, especially in heavy rains, which disrupts movement.
Earthquake

When the outer surface of the earth starts vibrating due to different movements in the internal parts of the earth, it is called an earthquake. An earthquake is created at one point in the earth, but its waves travel in all directions. Sometimes a large number of human lives are lost due to an earthquake. It destroys buildings, bridges and roads. It also affects the supply of water, gas and electricity.
Floods

When the level of water in rivers rises and rivers start overflowing due to heavy rains and the melting of snow on mountains, it is called a flood. It damages crops in the fields, and animals are drowned in floods. Human properties are also destroyed. Besides, diseases break out in flood-affected areas.
Safety Measures against Floods

People must be warned before the flood. • Those places where there is danger of flood should be vacated in an emergency. • People should keep themselves away from electric wires and poles in floods. • As flood water causes diseases, we should keep ourselves away from flood water. • Water, food and first aid should be provided.

Safety Measures against Earthquakes

Buildings must be vacated during an earthquake. • An earthquake can be followed by another earthquake or its aftershocks; therefore, we should be ready to keep ourselves safe. • High-rise buildings should not be built in earthquake zones. • People should keep food, water and a first aid kit with them. • People should be trained to protect themselves during earthquakes so that they are well prepared in an emergency.
Safety Measures against Earthquakes

Consumer and Producer

Producers produce and provide goods and services. They are farmers and industrialists. Farmers grow crops and sell them. Industrialists make different products from raw materials and sell them in markets. Those who buy and use goods and services are called consumers. A consumer buys goods and services with money.
Inflation

The rate of continuous rise in the prices of goods and services is called inflation. The main reason for inflation is the devaluation of currency. The value of a currency is obtained from the worth of the goods and services, which is called Gross Domestic Product (GDP). As GDP increases, the value of the currency increases. As GDP decreases, the value of the currency also decreases, which results in inflation.
Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
The total value of goods and services produced in a country in one year.
Inflation

One of the major reasons for inflation in Pakistan is the rise in the prices of petroleum products. Pakistan buys these products from international markets. In Pakistan, the prices of petrol and diesel rise with the rise of the prices of petroleum in the international market. As a result, the cost of transportation increases, due to which the prices of fruits, vegetables and other things increase.
Inflation
Prices of goods also increase when things are imported from foreign countries due to their low production in the country.

Cost Push Inflation

The production charges of a product are called cost. Cost push inflation is the result of an increase in the production charges of goods. For example, you own a bicycle production factory. You make bicycles from plastic and steel. If the prices of steel and plastic increase, the price of the bicycle will also increase.
Demand Pull Inflation

The intention to purchase together with purchasing power is called demand. Demand pull inflation emerges when things fall short of demand. For example, you go to the market to buy a computer. There are only ten computers available, while the buyers are more than ten. In such a case, you agree to give even more money to buy a computer. The shopkeeper increases the price of computers to avail this opportunity.

Money is an important part of our life. It is also called paisa or wealth. We can fulfil our basic needs with it, such as food, clothes, housing etc. Besides these basic needs, money is also a source of business and education. It is also used for fulfilling one's needs and desires.

Think and tell: if there were no money today, how would people do business? • What do you buy with pocket money?
Evolution of Money
People did not use money for business in ancient times. There was no system of currency or money. At that time, people used to exchange things with each other. It was called the barter system.
Barter System

The exchange of things in buying and selling is called the barter system. It is an old system of dealing. People used to give surplus things to others in exchange for things they needed. For example, if a person needed clothes, he would give wheat or rice to a weaver in exchange for clothes. People also exchanged chickens, goats etc. for buying things of their needs. The barter system continued for a long time.
Barter System
Then, in about 1200 BC, people started using seashells and precious stones for buying and selling. Metals like bronze and copper were also discovered.
Stop and Tell
Why did people start using money instead of the barter system?
Metallic Coins

Bronze and copper coins were made in China in about 1000 BC. They are considered the original form of present-day coins. These coins had holes so that they could be collected in the form of a chain. Round coins of the present-day form were made in Lydia (in present-day Turkey) in about 600 BC. The methods of coin making were also copied by other nations.
Metallic Coins

They improved bronze, copper and gold coins and started using them. Metallic coins were heavy, and it was difficult to take them from one place to another. At last, they were replaced by paper currency.
Leather Money
Pieces of leather were used as money in about 118 BC in China. These pieces were made of the skin of white deer.
For Teachers

Demonstrate the barter system practically for buying and selling to the students for better understanding. Tell the stages of the evolution of money from the barter system to currency notes in the form of a story to the students. Tell them that earlier people used seashells for purchasing things. Ten seashells were equal to one doit. After seashells, they used coins and then paper currency.
Paper Currency

Paper currency was introduced in China in about 806 AD. Other nations also started making paper currency with the passage of time. Paper currency had been introduced in other parts of the world by the end of the eighteenth century. Now paper currency is being replaced by polymer notes. Australia was the first country to introduce polymer notes, and Indonesia also adopted them early.
Plastic Money

Banks introduced credit cards and debit cards in the twentieth century. They put an end to the use of hard cash to some extent. The modern period is digital. Now people can easily transfer money to each other electronically through computerised channels. Therefore, people do not keep money in their pockets anymore.
History of Currency in the Subcontinent

Coin making started at the beginning of the sixth century BC in the subcontinent. These coins were called 'Pana'. These coins were made of silver. They had no definite shape. They had different signs on them. • This region was ruled by different nations, such as Persians, Turks, Arabs, Greeks and British. These nations and governments introduced coins of different shapes and signs.
History of Currency in the Subcontinent

• This region was conquered by the Arabs in 712 AD. The emperors of Delhi and, after them, the Mughal rulers introduced their coins. They replaced symbols with Islamic writings on them. Coins made of pure gold and silver were used during the thirteenth century. These gold and silver coins were called ashrafi. • The British occupied the subcontinent in 1857. They issued coins made of silver, bronze and nickel.
History of Currency in the Subcontinent
These included the rupee and the anna. These coins had pictures of British rulers on them. The rupee was made the official currency at that time.
Did you know?
Sher Shah Suri introduced a silver coin which was called the rupee.
Currency

We use money in the form of coins or paper currency for dealing in our daily life. In economics, it is called currency. Each country has its own currency, such as the currency of Pakistan is the rupee.

Role and Importance of Money
Money has special importance in human life.
Role and Importance of Money

Every person depends on money for his or her basic needs, such as food, clothes and housing. Money is also used for fulfilling many other needs and desires. • Money is also used for purchasing land and gold, getting education and doing business.
Role and Importance of Money

We not only buy different things with money but also avail different services; for example, the services of mechanics and masons are availed in exchange for money. • Money improves the standard of life.
Bank
A bank is a financial and commercial institution. People keep their surplus money in a bank for safety. People open accounts in banks and keep their money in them. Besides:
Bank

Traders, industrialists, agriculturists and other needy people get loans from banks. • People can easily transfer their money from one city to another or from one country to another. • Bills of electricity, Sui gas and telephone are also paid through banks. • Applications for Hajj and Umrah are also submitted through banks. • People keep their jewellery and important documents in bank lockers for safety.
Bank
All these services are provided by commercial banks.
Foreign Exchange Reserves
Foreign currency, gold and other important financial assets kept in the central bank of a country are called the foreign exchange reserves of that country.
Let's do something new!
Do research with your friend to find out and tell who issues currency and how it is issued.
State Bank of Pakistan

Every country has a central bank which supervises the whole economy of the country. The name of Pakistan's central bank is the State Bank of Pakistan. It was founded in 1948. Its headquarters is in Karachi. It supervises the financial activities of all other banks in Pakistan and makes policies for them. It also issues currency notes. It is the custodian of foreign exchange reserves.
State Bank of Pakistan
It keeps a balance between exports and imports in order to secure foreign exchange reserves.

Ask students to get information from their parents, sisters, brothers or relatives about their banks. Take them on a study tour to a bank and tell them about its activities.
